_readme: The role vocabulary, and role -> template mapping. Machine-readable so template coverage is a computed fact rather than a sentence in a README that goes stale. catalog.py reads this and fails CI if a declared template is missing, which is what stopped the previous 'the four written are the ones the tooling depends on' claim (there were seven) from happening again. A role whose template lives in another plugin declares that plugin in 'externalPlugin'. A role whose 'template' is null has NO scaffolding: that is reported as an uncovered role, never counted as coverage, because a role registered with nothing behind it reads exactly like a covered one unless something says otherwise.
_schemaNote: Each entry under 'roles' is an object: {group, template, archetypes, workspace, why?}. It was a bare filename string until the archetype vocabulary landed (RFC-0002 §3c/§3d, issue #95); a string would have had nowhere to say which project kinds a role applies to, and 'applies to everything' is the assumption that made /bootstrap-api-docs emit an empty flows document for a package.

archetypes._readme: The project kinds a role can apply to. This list is the vocabulary: a projectKind outside it is a refusal, never a default. Guessing 'service' for a package is the clean-vs-could-not-look ambiguity the governing principle forbids. Both kinds here were measured on real repositories before they were named (a PHP parser package and its REST API sibling); a third kind is added when a third repository is measured, never speculatively.
archetypes._workspaceNote: 'workspace' is deliberately NOT a kind. A monorepo is a container OF archetypes; as a kind it would force a repo holding a service and a package to pick one and be wrong either way. It is an orthogonal boolean on the profile, and each role's 'workspace' field says whether it resolves once at workspace root or once per member.
archetypes.library: A published package consumed by other repositories - a public API surface, a versioning story, consumers who pin by tag.
archetypes.service: A deployed data or API service - routes, request/response contracts, error envelopes, rate limits, caching.

groups._readme: Which part of the vocabulary a role came from, as distinct from which archetypes it applies to. 'group' is a fixed partition and answers 'how big is the library extension'; 'archetypes' can mark one role usable under several kinds and answers 'what should this repository have'. Collapsing the two would lose one of those questions.
groups.any: Applies to any archetype and belongs to none.
groups.core: Universal: every repository kind this suite has measured needs it. Present in substance everywhere, which is what 'core' means here.
groups.library: Came from the library archetype; not applicable to a service unless marked.

applicability.expected: The archetype is incomplete without this document — its absence is a finding.
applicability.optional: Applies, but its absence is a legitimate project choice, not a gap.
applicability.na: Does not apply to this archetype. Never propose it, never report it missing.

aliases._readme: Old role name -> current role name. resolve.py resolves through this in both directions so a consumer manifest written before a rename keeps working, and a skill written after it keeps working against an un-migrated manifest. A rename with no alias is a silent unmapped role, which is exit 2 at best and a wrong file at worst.

entry-point.why: Every repository has a read-this-first. Without it a skill has no starting node. Renamed from 'instructions' (issue #95) because that name reads as agent-instructions.

documentation-rules.why: The role that keeps every other role honest. Every repo with docs has rules about docs.

decisions.why: Universal by the widest margin of any role measured.

backlog.why: The docs work that has been seen but not done, so it is not lost.

contributing.why: Universal role, archetype-specific spine: add an endpoint versus add a parser method.

rfc.why: In the core because a package's breaking changes need a proposal format before they need a release; a service can carry the same content informally.

brief.why: The intake document for a client-facing project (house-style's onboarding). Optional everywhere: absent from packages measured, where scope is the README.

api.why: The public surface itself. Both kinds have one: endpoints for a service, methods and models for a package.

api-standard.why: Cross-cutting contract conventions: the response envelope, the error shape, versioning. A service without one answers the same question differently on every route; a package states it once in its API doc.

builds.why: How this repository's checks actually run. Absent here, 'it passes CI' is hearsay.

deployment.why: A package is consumed, not deployed; an absent deployment story for a service is a gap, so 'na' and 'expected' rather than optional in both directions.

production-readiness.why: The production checklist for a deployed service (and, optionally, for a package whose consumers run it in theirs).

changelog.why: Load-bearing for a package whose consumers pin by tag; a service's consumers see changes the moment they land.

deprecations.why: The running ledger, deliberately separate from the release process that governs it. Services deprecate endpoints too, but the API standard carries that story until it outgrows it.

common-mistakes.why: The pitfalls a contributor will otherwise rediscover the hard way.

release.why: How a version gets cut and published. Both kinds ship versions; a service's are API versions, a package's are tags consumers pin.

public-roadmap.why: Optional everywhere: a legitimate project choice, not a gap.

postmortem.why: Zero instances across the repositories measured, so optional everywhere rather than expected anywhere.

pr.why: The PR process is org scope, not universal. It ships with the house-style plugin so a project installing backend-suite alone does not inherit the org's PR conventions. This is also why it cannot be a universal-core role: putting it there would re-import into the universal plugin the org literal the CI rules forbid.
